title: Mechanisms and applications of aflatoxin degradation by engineered Lactobacillus plantarum in food systems
content:
Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1), a highly toxic mycotoxin contaminating cereal grains, oil-based foods, fruits, and flour, poses a severe threat to global food safety. This study successfully engineered and validated a recombinant Lactobacillus plantarum strain capable of secreting CotA tyrosinase. The enzyme mediates AFB1 degradation by disrupting its lactone ring structure, converting the toxin into low-toxicity metabolites (AFQ1 and epi-AFQ1), which significantly reduce cytotoxicity. This biocontrol approach offers an efficient and safe solution for AFB1 detoxification in fruits and flour, highlighting promising industrial applications for ensuring food safety.


Abstract

Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is a highly toxic mycotoxin that contaminates grain and oil foods. Its strong carcinogenicity poses a serious threat to global food safety. Existing biological detoxification methods have limitations such as poor enzyme stability or insufficient antimicrobial efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for synergistic solutions with both efficient degradation and mould inhibition capabilities. This study aims to construct an engineered Lactobacillus plantarum strain that secretes Spore coat protein A laccase (CotA laccase) and systematically evaluate its AFB1 degradation ability and industrial application potential. The engineered strain Lp-CotA was successfully constructed using genetic engineering technology. Mechanistic studies revealed that the CotA enzyme breaks the lactone ring structure of AFB1, converting it into low-toxicity products AFQ1 and epi-AFQ1, thereby reducing cytotoxicity. Application experiments showed that the engineered strain achieved over 85% AFB1 degradation within 72 h. In flour, it exhibited preventive and repair effects against AFB1, effectively inhibited mould growth, and maximally preserved nutritional components. In apple preservation, the engineered strain controlled the decay rate to 10% with an AFB1 degradation rate of 85.9%. This research provides an efficient and safe solution for the biological control of AFB1 in grains, fruits, and vegetables, with important industrial application prospects.
